question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z(x+y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z(x+y))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+y))\,k \\  & =z\,i+z\,j+(x+y)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & ={e}^{t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$
